method_note: Web search and fetched page text only. Shell egress to source hosts was refused (HTTP 403 on CONNECT: gutenberg.org, archive.org, wikisource.org), and the fetch tool returns a model-summarised page, not source bytes, and would not return chant lines verbatim. No source file was downloaded or hashed in this pass and no transcription was compared word for word. A verdict below is a rights/suitability finding, not a transcription check.

verdicts.USABLE_VERIFIED: genre, transcription, translation and reuse basis all verified; a lesson and attribution record exist
verdicts.NO_TEXT_TO_TEACH: source examined; prints no chant/praise text for the target genre
verdicts.NOT_SUITABLE: text exists but is a different genre or not a traditional text
verdicts.REJECTED_PROVENANCE: text exists in an openly licensed work but its origin, transcription or the right to reuse it is not established
verdicts.NOT_REUSABLE: text exists and the genre fits, but no licence or permission covers reuse
verdicts.UNVERIFIED_LEAD: may contain usable text; could not be read in this environment

genres.best_lead: YT-03 (Johnson 1921), unreadable here; a rights-cleared text from a chanter or Kolawole's recordings
genres.missing: A named Ṣàngó pípè passage with performer or collector, date and place, tone-marked Yoruba transcription, a named translation, and a written or licence basis for reuse.

genres.best_lead: none found; no candidate prints Ọya pípè text
genres.missing: Any Ọya pípè passage with the same provenance, transcription, translation and reuse basis as above.

genres.best_lead: YT-09 (Olajubu 1977 chant, genre fits, rights not cleared)
genres.missing: Written permission from the rights holder of one named iwì egúngún chant (or a chanter's own text), with its transcription and translation checked; separately, an owner decision on whether èsà egúngún may stand for the scheme's iwì egúngún.

sources.source: A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), Chapter II (Chief Gods), via the sacred-texts mirror
sources.rights_basis: 1894 publication; public domain by age (not separately verified for every jurisdiction)
sources.finding: Gives Yoruba names and epithets with English glosses (for example Jakuta, Magba, Afefe). Priests' chants, salutations and imprecations are printed in English only.
sources.unblock: none; the book does not print Yoruba chant text for these genres

sources.source: A. B. Ellis (1894), Chapter VI (Egungun, Oro, Abiku, and Various Superstitions), same mirror
sources.finding: No Egúngún chant. One Yoruba saying with translation (a warriors' saying) and single glossed words only.

sources.source: Samuel Johnson, The History of the Yorubas (1921), Internet Archive scan
sources.rights_basis: Author died 1901 (existing OB-03 record). The 1921 edition was published posthumously and edited by Obadiah Johnson; his status and the edition's editorial matter were not checked.
sources.finding: Only the first ~100,000 characters of the PDF text (partway through Chapter I) could be read; the fetch tool offers no offset. Nothing about Ṣàngó, Ọya or Egúngún appears in that part. A Wikisource page-level transcription exists but its page could not be retrieved. The religion and Ṣàngó chapters are unread, so whether the book prints any chant text for these genres is unknown.
sources.unblock: A reader with the full text checks the Ṣàngó, Ọya and Egúngún passages and reports page numbers, whether Yoruba text is printed with a translation, and the genre the author names. Without printed Yoruba text there is nothing to teach as text study.

sources.source: Kolawole (2023), Variations in the application of the components of the oral performance to Yoruba chants, Tydskrif vir Letterkunde 60(3):75-89
sources.rights_basis: CC BY-SA 4.0 per the article page; the PDF front matter says only 'Creative Commons Attribution License' (existing discrepancy, kept)
sources.finding: Carried from the 19 October 2026 full read recorded in OB-03: names Ṣàngó pípè, Ọya pípè and èsà egúngún but prints lines for Èṣù pípè, ofò, ìyẹ̀rẹ̀ Ifá, ìjálá and oríkì orílẹ̀ only. Not re-read in this pass.
sources.unblock: Written permission to use the author's recordings or transcriptions of the target forms, if they exist

sources.source: Aransi Ayoola Oladunke (2024), Yoruba chanters' performance strategies, Journal of Languages, Linguistics and Literary Studies 4(2)
sources.rights_basis: Article states CC BY-SA 4.0 (the page's wording reads 'Creative Common Attribution (CC BY-SA 4.0)').
sources.finding: Prints eight Yoruba chant excerpts with English, one labelled èsà (about eleven lines, Humour section, near p. 103; page numbers approximate). Ṣàngó pípè and Ọya pípè are not mentioned. The article gives no performer, place, date or collection method for any excerpt and no chanter consent statement, and it does not say that èsà egúngún is iwì egúngún.
sources.unblock: The author states where the èsà excerpt came from (own recording, or another published work) and, if from another work, who holds the rights; a source that identifies the genre as iwì egúngún.

sources.source: Akinbo, Samuel, Alaga and Akingbade (2022), An acoustic study of vocal expression in two genres of Yoruba oral poetry, Frontiers in Communication 7:1029400
sources.finding: Compares ìjálá and èsà. Its four-line example is a poem composed by a co-author and chanted by one student for the study; it is not a traditional text.

sources.source: González and Oludare (2022), The Speech Surrogacy Systems of the Yoruba Dùndún and Bàtá Drums, Frontiers in Communication 6:652542
sources.finding: No chant lines for the target genres; researcher-composed test sentences and one proverb.

sources.source: Akinyemi (2026), Myth, Legend, and Poetics of Heroism in Ọba Kòso and Ṣàngó, in Echoes of Yoruba Oral Traditions in Contemporary Nigerian Dramaturgy (Palgrave Macmillan)
sources.rights_basis: Not open access; paywalled; copyright line 'under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG'
sources.finding: The notes cite a Ṣàngó chant excerpt but the page prints neither lines nor translation. Full chapter not accessible.
sources.unblock: Publisher and author permission for a named excerpt

sources.source: africanpoems.net, 'But for Death' (page credits Oludare Olajubu, 'Iwi Egungun Chants: an Introduction', in Forms of Folklore in Africa, ed. Bernth Lindfors, Texas, 1977)
sources.rights_basis: None stated. The site gives no licence, no translator and no reuse permission. The underlying 1977 publication is not open licensed.
sources.finding: Genre fits: the page describes the poem as an Iwì Egúngún chant performed by masked dancers. The text was deliberately not copied or checked in this pass.
sources.unblock: Written permission from the 1977 rights holder (publisher and/or author's estate), then transcription and translation checked against the book, not the website.
